title: Neanderthal Glue May Have Doubled as Germ-Fighting Medicine
summary:
Neanderthals were ancient humans who lived in Europe and parts of Asia long ago. They made a sticky substance called birch tar by heating the bark of birch trees. Archaeologists have found traces of it at many Neanderthal sites, often still stuck to stone tools. For decades, scientists thought Neanderthals used birch tar mainly as glue, to attach stone blades and points to wooden handles.

A new study suggests birch tar may have had a second job: helping protect wounds from infection.

Researchers from the University of Cologne in Germany, the University of Oxford in England, the University of Liège in Belgium and Cape Breton University in Canada did the study. It was published in the science journal PLOS One.

The team made its own birch tar using kinds of trees that grew during Neanderthal times. Instead of modern factory methods, they copied techniques that archaeologists think Neanderthals used. In one method, they sealed birch bark in a pit underground and heated it with little or no air. In a simpler method, they burned bark next to a stone, and tar collected on the cooler stone surface.

Then they tested the tar against bacteria. Every sample they made was able to slow the growth of Staphylococcus aureus, a type of bacteria that often causes wound infections. Some kinds of this germ have become hard to treat with modern antibiotics.

The idea came partly from other clues. Traditional societies around the world have used birch tar as medicine, and there is growing evidence that Neanderthals used plants and cared for one another.

"There is also growing evidence of medicinal practices and the use of plants among Neanderthals," said Tjaark Siemssen, who led the study. The results suggest Neanderthals may have had a useful natural medicine.
why_it_matters: The study suggests Neanderthals may have understood more about healing than once thought. It also shows how experiments today can test ideas about life long ago.

background_read: Neanderthals were close relatives of modern humans who made stone tools and lived through ice age times.
Birch tar is made by heating birch bark, and it works like a strong natural glue.
Archaeologists learn about ancient people by studying tools and leftovers, and scientists sometimes recreate old methods to test ideas.
Some bacteria can infect wounds, and today doctors often treat those infections with antibiotics.
